summary: This bill establishes a tax on greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels, industrial processes, and certain products, using the generated revenue to fund infrastructure, environmental solutions, and assistance for displaced energy workers, while also imposing sanctions on Russia, restricting stock trading by House members, and addressing other policy areas.

scores.thoughts: Title I establishes the RISE Trust Fund, appropriating 75% of greenhouse gas tax revenues to it, and then allocates these funds to various programs including the Highway Trust Fund, weatherization, displaced energy workers, Airport and Airway Trust Fund, Leaking Underground Storage Trust Fund, Abandoned Mine Reclamation Fund, coastal flooding mitigation, energy research, carbon capture, and State grants. Title II also directly appropriates funds to the National Cancer Institute. These provisions clearly increase government spending across multiple sectors.

Title I of the bill imposes a new tax on greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels, industrial processes, and certain product uses, with rates starting at $35 per metric ton and increasing annually. It also repeals federal motor vehicle and aviation fuel taxes, which would reduce some existing taxes, but the introduction of a broad carbon tax is a significant new tax. The bill also includes border tax adjustments on imports and rebates for exports, which are essentially taxes and subsidies related to carbon intensity.

The bill establishes new taxes (carbon tax) and repeals some existing ones (fuel taxes), but primarily focuses on allocating the new tax revenues to various spending programs and trust funds rather than explicitly directing them towards national debt reduction. While the new carbon tax could generate significant revenue, the bill immediately appropriates 75% of it to new spending initiatives, indicating a focus on investment rather than debt reduction.

The bill's largest component (Title I) creates a new carbon tax generating substantial revenues that are fully appropriated to new or expanded spending programs via the RISE Trust Fund. Additional new spending is authorized outside those revenues (e.g., 25% increase in NCI funding for five years and extension of ALS survivor benefits). A small fiscal commission title pushes toward deficit reduction, but the overall thrust is using new revenues and appropriations to advance multiple unrelated priorities rather than net deficit reduction.
